entries.ac57647c20a2ba77709418029eef460abe38405e: <div sID="gen19110" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="36" osisID="Ezek.36" sID="Ezek.36"/> <div eID="gen19110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19111" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19112" type="x-p"/> We have done with Mount Seir, and left it desolate, and likely to continue so, and must now turn ourselves, with the prophet, to the mountains of Israel, which we find desolate too, but hope before we have done with the chapter to leave in better plight. Here are two distinct prophecies in this chapter:—I. Here is one that seems chiefly to relate to the temporal estate of the Jews, wherein their present deplorable condition is described and the triumphs of their neighbours in it; but it is promised that their grievances shall be all redressed and that in due time they shall be settled again in their own land, in the midst of peace and plenty, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.1-Ezek.36.15">ver. 1-15</reference>. II. Here is another that seems chiefly to concern their spiritual estate, wherein they are reminded of their former sins and God's judgments upon them, to humble them for their sins and under God's mighty hand, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.16-Ezek.36.20">ver. 16-20</reference>. But it is promised, 1. That God would glorify himself in showing mercy to them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.21-Ezek.36.24">ver. 21-24</reference>. 2. That he would sanctify them, by giving them his grace and fitting them for his service; and this for his own name's sake and in answer to their prayers, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25-Ezek.36.38">ver. 25-38</reference>.
entries.e5731859f4791a32cd13bf9422bacf28f1b4cda9: <div eID="gen19112" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19111" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Compassion for Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19113" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Also, thou son of man, prophesy unto the mountains of Israel, and say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because the enemy hath said against you, Aha, even the ancient high places are ours in possession: <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because they have made <hi type="italic">you</hi> desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that ye might be a possession unto the residue of the heathen, and ye are taken up in the lips of talkers, and <hi type="italic">are</hi> an infamy of the people: <hi type="super">4</hi> Therefore, ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> to the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys, to the desolate wastes, and to the cities that are forsaken, which became a prey and derision to the residue of the heathen that <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about; <hi type="super">5</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Surely in the fire of my jealousy have I spoken against the residue of the heathen, and against all Idumea, which have appointed my land into their possession with the joy of all <hi type="italic">their</hi> heart, with despiteful minds, to cast it out for a prey. <hi type="super">6</hi> Prophesy therefore concerning the land of Israel, and say unto the mountains, and to the hills, to the rivers, and to the valleys, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I have spoken in my jealousy and in my fury, because ye have borne the shame of the heathen: <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I have lifted up mine hand, Surely the heathen that <hi type="italic">are</hi> about you, they shall bear their shame. <hi type="super">8</hi> But ye, O mountains of Israel, ye shall shoot forth your branches, and yield your fruit to my people of Israel; for they are at hand to come. <hi type="super">9</hi> For, behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> for you, and I will turn unto you, and ye shall be tilled and sown: <hi type="super">10</hi> And I will multiply men upon you, all the house of Israel, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all of it: and the cities shall be inhabited, and the wastes shall be builded: <hi type="super">11</hi> And I will multiply upon you man and beast; and they shall increase and bring fruit: and I will settle you after your old estates, and will do better <hi type="italic">unto you</hi> than at your beginnings: and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> Yea, I will cause men to walk upon you, <hi type="italic">even</hi> my people Israel; and they shall possess thee, and thou shalt be their inheritance, and thou shalt no more henceforth bereave them <hi type="italic">of men.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Because they say unto you, Thou <hi type="italic">land</hi> devourest up men, and hast bereaved thy nations; <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore thou shalt devour men no more, neither bereave thy nations any more, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> Neither will I cause <hi type="italic">men</hi> to hear in thee the shame of the heathen any more, neither shalt thou bear the reproach of the people any more, neither shalt thou cause thy nations to fall any more, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen19113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19114" type="x-p"/> The prophet had been ordered to set his face <hi type="italic">towards the mountains of Israel</hi> and <hi type="italic">prophesy against them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.6.2">ch. vi. 2</reference>. Then God was coming forth to contend with his people; but now that God is returning in mercy to them he must speak good words and comfortable words to these mountains, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.1">v. 1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.4">again v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">You mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord;</hi> and what he says to them he says <hi type="italic">to the hills, to the rivers, to the valleys, to the desolate wastes</hi> in the country, and to the cities <hi type="italic">that are forsaken,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.4">v. 4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.6">again v. 6</reference>. The people were gone, some one way and some another; nothing remained there to be spoken to but the places, the mountains and valleys; these the Chaldeans could not carry away with them. <hi type="italic">The earth abides for ever.</hi> Now, to show the mercy God had in reserve for the people, he is to speak of him as having a dormant kindness for the place, which, if the Lord had been pleased for ever to abandon, he would not have called upon to <hi type="italic">hear the word of the Lord,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">would he as at this time have shown it such things as these.</hi> Here is, <div eID="gen19114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19115" type="x-p"/> I. The compassionate notice God takes of the present deplorable condition of the land of Israel. It has become both a <hi type="italic">prey</hi> and a <hi type="italic">derision to the heathen that are round about,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.4">v. 4</reference>. 1. It has become a prey to them; and they are all enriched with the plunder of it. When the Chaldeans had conquered them all their neighbours flew to the spoil as to a shipwreck, every one thinking all his own that he could lay his hands on (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that you might be a possession to the heathen,</hi> to the <hi type="italic">residue</hi> of them, even such as had themselves narrowly escaped the like desolation. No one thought it any crime to strip an Israelite. <hi type="italic">Turba Romæ sequitur fortunam ut semper—The mob of Rome still praise the elevated and despise the fallen.</hi> It is the common dry, when a man is down, <hi type="italic">Down with him.</hi> 2. It has become a derision to them. They took all they had and laughed at them when they had done. <hi type="italic">The enemy said, "Aha! even the ancient high places are ours in possession,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.2">v. 2</reference>. Neither the antiquity, nor the dignity, neither the sanctity nor the fortifications, of the land of Israel, are its security, but we have become masters of it all." The more honours that land had been adorned with, and the greater figure it had made among the nations, the more pride and pleasure did they take in making a spoil of it, which is an instance of a base and sordid spirit; for the more glorious and prosperity was the more piteous is the adversity. God takes notice of it here as an aggravation of the present calamity of Israel: <hi type="italic">You are taken up in the lips of talkers and are an infamy of the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.3">v. 3</reference>. All the talk of the country about was concerning the overthrow of the Jewish nation; and every one that spoke of it had some peevish ill-natured reflection or other upon them. They were the <hi type="italic">scorning of those that were at ease and the contempt of the proud,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Ps. cxxiii. 4</reference>. There are some that are noted for talkers, that have something to say of every body, but cannot find in their hearts to speak well of any body; God's people, among such people, were sure to be a reproach when the crown had fallen from their head. Thus it was the lot of Christianity, in its suffering days, to be <hi type="italic">every where spoken against.</hi> <div eID="gen19115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19116" type="x-p"/> II. The expressions of God's just displeasure against those who triumphed in the desolations of the land of Israel, as many of its neighbours did, even the residue of the brethren, and Idumea particularly. Let us see, 1. How they dealt with the Israel of God. They carved out large possessions to themselves out of their land, out of God's land; for so indeed it was: "<hi type="italic">They have appointed my land into their possession</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.5">v. 5</reference>), and so not only invaded their neighbour's property, but intrenched upon God's prerogative." It was the holy land which they laid their sacrilegious hands upon. They did not own any dependence upon God, as the God of that land, nor acknowledge any remaining interest that Israel had in it, but <hi type="italic">cast it out for a prey,</hi> as if they had won it in a lawful war. And this they did without any dread of God and his judgments and without any compassion for Israel and their calamities, but with the <hi type="italic">joy of all their hearts,</hi> because they got by it, and <hi type="italic">with despiteful minds</hi> to Israel that lost by it. Increasing wealth, by right or wrong, is all the joy of a worldly heart; and the calamities of God's people are all the joy of a despiteful mind. And those that had not an opportunity of making a prey of God's people made a reproach of them; so that they were <hi type="italic">the shame of the heathen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.6">v. 6</reference>. Every body ridiculed them and made a jest of them; and the truth is they had by their own sin made themselves vile; so that God was righteous herein, but men were unrighteous and very barbarous. 2. How God would deal with those who were thus in word and deed abusive to his people. He has <hi type="italic">spoken against the heathen;</hi> he has passed sentence upon them; he has determined to reckon with them for it, and this <hi type="italic">in the fire of his jealousy,</hi> both for his own honour and for the honour of his people, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.5">v. 5</reference>. Having a <hi type="italic">love</hi> for both as <hi type="italic">strong as death,</hi> he has a <hi type="italic">jealousy</hi> for both as <hi type="italic">cruel as the grave.</hi> They spoke in their malice against God's people, and he will speak in his jealousy against them; and it is easy to say which will speak most powerfully. God will speak <hi type="italic">in his jealousy and in his fury,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.6">v. 6</reference>. Fury is not in God; but he will exert his power against them and handle them as severely as men do when they are in a fury. He will so <hi type="italic">speak to them in his wrath as to vex them in his sore displeasure.</hi> What he says he will stand to, for it is backed with an oath. He has <hi type="italic">lifted up his hand</hi> and sworn by himself, has sworn and will not repent. And what is it that is said with so much heat, and yet with so much deliberation? It is this (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Surely the heathen that are about you, they shall bear their shame.</hi> Note, The righteous God, to whom vengeance belongs, will render shame for shame. Those that put contempt and reproach upon God's people will, sooner or later, have it <hi type="italic">burned upon themselves,</hi> perhaps in this world (either their follies or their calamities, their miscarriages or their mischances, shall be their reproach), at furthest in that day when all the impenitent shall <hi type="italic">rise to shame and everlasting contempt.</hi> <div eID="gen19116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19117" type="x-p"/> III. The promises of God's favour to his Israel and assurances given of great mercy God had in store for them. God takes occasion from the outrage and insolence of their enemies to show himself so much the more concerned for them and ready to do them good, as David hoped that God would recompense him good for Shimei's cursing him. <hi type="italic">Let them curse, but bless thou.</hi> In this way, as well as others, the enemies of God's people do them real service, even by the injuries they do them, against their will and beyond their intention. We shall have no reason to complain if, the more unkind men are, the more kind God is—if, the more kindly he speaks to us by his word and Spirit, the more kindly he acts for us in his providence. The prophet must say so to the <hi type="italic">mountains of Israel,</hi> which were now <hi type="italic">desolate and despised,</hi> that God is <hi type="italic">for them</hi> and will <hi type="italic">burn to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.9">v. 9</reference>. As the curse of God reaches the ground for man's sake, so does the blessing. Now that which is promised is, 1. That their rightful owners should return to the possession of them: <hi type="italic">My people Israel are at hand to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.8">v. 8</reference>. Though they are at a great distance from their own country, though they are dispersed in many countries, and though they are detained by the power of their enemies, yet they shall <hi type="italic">come again to their own border,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.17">Jer. xxxi. 17</reference>. The time is at hand for their return. Though there were above forty years of the seventy (perhaps fifty) yet remaining, it is spoken of as near, because it is sure, and there were some among them that should live to see it. A <hi type="italic">thousand years are</hi> with God but <hi type="italic">as one day.</hi> The mountains of Israel are now desolate; but God will <hi type="italic">cause men to walk upon them</hi> again, <hi type="italic">even his people Israel,</hi> not as travellers passing over them, but as inhabitants—not tenants, but freeholders: <hi type="italic">They shall possess thee,</hi> not for term of life, but for themselves and their heirs; <hi type="italic">thou shalt be their inheritance.</hi> It was a type of the heavenly Canaan, to which all God's children are heirs, every Israelite indeed, and into which they shall shortly be all brought together, out of the countries where they are now scattered. 2. That they should afford a plentiful comfortable maintenance for their owners at their return. When the land had <hi type="italic">enjoyed her sabbaths</hi> for so many years, it should be so much the more fruitful afterwards, as we should be after rest, especially a sabbath rest: <hi type="italic">You shall be tilled and sown</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.9">v. 9</reference>) and shall <hi type="italic">yield your fruit to my people Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, It is a blessing to the earth to be made serviceable to men, especially to good men, that will serve God with cheerfulness in the use of those good things which the earth serves up to them. 3. That the people of Israel should have not only a comfortable sustenance, but a comfortable settlement, in their own land: The <hi type="italic">cities shall be inhabited; the wastes shall be builded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.10">v. 10</reference>. And <hi type="italic">I will settle you after your old estates,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.11">v. 11</reference>. Their own sin had unsettled them, but now God's favour shall resettle them. When the prodigal son has become a penitent he is settled again in his father's house, according to his former estate. Bring hither the <hi type="italic">first robe,</hi> and put it on him. Nay, <hi type="italic">I will do better unto you</hi> now <hi type="italic">than at your beginnings.</hi> There is more joy for the sheep that is brought back than there would have been if it had never gone astray. And God sometimes multiplies his people's comforts in proportion to the <hi type="italic">time that he has afflicted them.</hi> Thus God blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning, and doubled to him all he had. 4. That the people, after their return, should be <hi type="italic">fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the land,</hi> so that it should not only be inhabited again, but as thickly inhabited, and as well peopled, as ever. God will bring back to it <hi type="italic">all the house of Israel, even all of it</hi> (observe what an emphasis is laid upon that, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.10">v. 10</reference>), all <hi type="italic">whose spirits God stirred up</hi> to return; and those only were reckoned of <hi type="italic">the house of Israel,</hi> the rest had cut themselves off from it; or, though but few, in comparison, returned at first, yet afterwards, at divers times, they <hi type="italic">all</hi> returned; and then (says God) <hi type="italic">I will multiply these men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">multiply man and beast; and they shall increase,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, God's kingdom in the world is a growing kingdom; and his church, though for a time it may be diminished, shall recover itself and be again replenished. 5. That the reproach long since cast up on the land of Israel by the evil spies, and of late revived, that <hi type="italic">it was a land that ate up the inhabitants</hi> of it by famine, sickness, and the sword, should be quite rolled away, and there should never be any more occasion for it. Canaan had got into a bad name. It had of old <hi type="italic">spued out the inhabitants</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.28">Lev. xviii. 28</reference>), the natives, the aborigines, which was turned to its reproach by those that should have put another construction upon it, <reference osisRef="Num.13.32">Num. xiii. 32</reference>. It had of late devoured the Israelites, and spued them out too; so that it was commonly said of it, It is a land which, instead of supporting its nations or tribes that inhabit it, <hi type="italic">bereaves</hi> them, <hi type="italic">overthrows</hi> them, and <hi type="italic">causes them to fall;</hi> it is a tenement which breaks all the tenants that come upon it. This character it had got among the neighbours; but God now promises that it shall be so no more: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt no more bereave them of men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.12">v. 12</reference>), shalt <hi type="italic">devour men no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.14">v. 14</reference>. But the inhabitants shall live to a good old age, and not have the number of their months cut off in the midst. Compare this with that promise, <reference osisRef="Zech.8.4">Zech. viii. 4</reference>. Note, God will take away the reproach of his people by taking away that which was the occasion of it. When the nation is made to flourish in peace, plenty, and power, then they <hi type="italic">hear no more the shame of the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.15">v. 15</reference>), especially when it is reformed; when sin, which is the reproach of any people, particularly of God's professing people, is taken away, then they <hi type="italic">hear no more the reproach of the people.</hi> Note, When God returns in mercy to a people that return to him in duty, all their grievances will be soon redressed and their honour retrieved.
entries.d838f237a9e55b43fe02826e1acf063e293e5e2f: <div eID="gen19117" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Compassion for Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19118" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">17</hi> Son of man, when the house of Israel dwelt in their own land, they defiled it by their own way and by their doings: their way was before me as the uncleanness of a removed woman. <hi type="super">18</hi> Wherefore I poured my fury upon them for the blood that they had shed upon the land, and for their idols <hi type="italic">wherewith</hi> they had polluted it: <hi type="super">19</hi> And I scattered them among the heathen, and they were dispersed through the countries: according to their way and according to their doings I judged them. <hi type="super">20</hi> And when they entered unto the heathen, whither they went, they profaned my holy name, when they said to them, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the people of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and are gone forth out of his land. <hi type="super">21</hi> But I had pity for mine holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the heathen, whither they went. <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I do not <hi type="italic">this</hi> for your sakes, O house of Israel, but for mine holy name's sake, which ye have profaned among the heathen, whither ye went. <hi type="super">23</hi> And I will sanctify my great name, which was profaned among the heathen, which ye have profaned in the midst of them; and the heathen shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes. <hi type="super">24</hi> For I will take you from among the heathen, and gather you out of all countries, and will bring you into your own land. <div eID="gen19118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19119" type="x-p"/> When God promised the poor captives a glorious return, in due time, to their own land, it was a great discouragement to their hopes that they were unworthy, utterly unworthy, of such a favour; therefore, to remove that discouragement, God here shows them that he would do it for them purely <hi type="italic">for his own name's sake,</hi> that he might be glorified in them and by them, that he might manifest and magnify his mercy and goodness, that attribute which of all others is most his glory. And, the restoration of that people being typical of our redemption by Christ, this is intended further to show that the ultimate end aimed at in our salvation, to which all the steps of it were made subservient, was the glory of God. To this end Christ directed all he did in that short prayer, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name;</hi> and God declared it was his end in all he did in the immediate answer given to that prayer, by a voice from heaven: <hi type="italic">I have glorified it, and I will glorify it yet again,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.28">John xii. 28</reference>. Now observe here, <div eID="gen19119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19120" type="x-p"/> I. How God's name had suffered both by the sins and by the miseries of Israel; and this was more to be regretted than all their sorrow, which they had brought upon themselves; for the honour of God lies nearer the hearts of good men than any interests of their own. 1. God's glory had been injured by the sin of Israel when they were in their own land, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.17">v. 17</reference>. It was a good land, a holy land, a land that had the eye of God upon it. <hi type="italic">But they defiled it by their own way,</hi> their wicked way; that is <hi type="italic">our own</hi> way, the way of our own choice; and we ourselves must bear the blame and shame of it. The sin of a people defiles their land, renders it abominable to God and uncomfortable to themselves; so that they cannot have any holy communion with him nor with one another. What was unclean might not be made use of. By the abuse of the gifts of God's bounty to us we forfeit the use of them; and, the mind and conscience being defiled with guilt, no comfort is allowed us, <hi type="italic">nothing is pure</hi> to us. Their way in the eye of God was like the pollution of a woman during the days of her separation, which shut her out from the sanctuary and made very things she touched ceremonially unclean, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.19">Lev. xv. 19</reference>. Sin is that <hi type="italic">abominable thing which the Lord hates,</hi> and which he cannot endure to look upon. They <hi type="italic">shed blood</hi> and <hi type="italic">worshipped idols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.18">v. 18</reference>) and with those sins <hi type="italic">defiled the land.</hi> For this God <hi type="italic">poured out his fury</hi> upon them, <hi type="italic">scattered them among the heathen.</hi> Their own land was sick of them, and they were sent into other lands. Herein God was righteous, and was justified in what he did; none could say that he did them any wrong, nay, he did justice to his own honour, for he <hi type="italic">judged them according to their way and according to their doings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.19">v. 19</reference>. And yet, the matter being not rightly understood, he was not glorified in it; for the enemies did say, as Moses pleaded the Egyptians would say if he had destroyed them in the wilderness, that <hi type="italic">for mischief he brought them forth.</hi> Their neighbours considered them rather as a holy people than as a sinful people, and therefore took occasion from the calamities they were in, instead of glorifying God, as they might justly have done, to reproach him and put contempt upon him; and God's name was <hi type="italic">continually every day blasphemed</hi> by their oppressors, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Isa. lii. 5</reference>. 2. When they <hi type="italic">entered into the land of the heathen</hi> God had no glory by them there; but, on the contrary, his holy name was profaned, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.20">v. 20</reference>. (1.) It was profaned by the sins of Israel; they were no credit to their profession wherever they went, but, on the contrary, a reproach to it. The <hi type="italic">name of God</hi> and his holy religion was <hi type="italic">blasphemed through them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.24">Rom. ii. 24</reference>. When those that pretended to be in relation to God, in covenant and communion with him, were found corrupt in their morals, slaves to their appetites and passions, dishonest in their dealings, and false to their words and the trust reposed in them, the enemies of the Lord had thereby great occasion given them to blaspheme, especially when they quarrelled with their God for correcting them, than which nothing could be more scandalous. (2.) It was profaned by the sufferings of Israel; for from them the enemies of God took occasion to reproach God, as unable to protect his own worshippers and to make good his own grants. They said, in scorn, "<hi type="italic">These are the people of the land,</hi> these wicked people (you see he could not keep them in their obedience to his precepts), these <hi type="italic">miserable people</hi>—you see he could not keep them in the enjoyment of his favours. These are <hi type="italic">the people that came out of Jehovah's land,</hi> they are the very scum of the nations. Are these those that had statues so righteous whose lives are so unrighteous? Is this the nation that is so much celebrated for a <hi type="italic">wise and understanding people,</hi> and that is said to have <hi type="italic">God so nigh unto them?</hi> Do these belong to that brave, that holy nation, who appear here so vile, so abject?" Thus God sold his people and did not <hi type="italic">increase his wealth by their price,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.12">Ps. xliv. 12</reference>. The reproach they were under reflected upon him. <div eID="gen19120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19121" type="x-p"/> II. Let us now see how God would retrieve his honour, secure it, and advance it, by working a great reformation upon them and then working a great salvation for them. He would have <hi type="italic">scattered them among the heathen, were it not that he feared the wrath of the enemy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.26-Deut.32.27">Deut. xxxii. 26, 27</reference>. But, though they were unworthy of his compassion, yet <hi type="italic">he had pity for his own holy name,</hi> and a thousand pities it was that that should be trampled upon and abused. He looked with compassion on his own honour, which lay bleeding among the heathen, on that jewel which was trodden into the dirt, which <hi type="italic">the house of Israel,</hi> even in the land of their captivity, <hi type="italic">had profaned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.21">v. 21</reference>. In pity to that God brought them out from the heathen, because their sins were more scandalous there than they had been in their own land. "Therefore I <hi type="italic">will gather you out of all countries and bring you into your own land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.24">v. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Not for your sake,</hi> because you are worthy of such a favour, for you are most unworthy, but <hi type="italic">for my holy name's sake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.22">v. 22</reference>), that <hi type="italic">I may sanctify my great name,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.23">v. 23</reference>. Observe, by the way, God's holy name is his great name. His holiness is his greatness; so he reckons it himself. Nor does any thing make a man truly great but being truly good, and partaking of God's holiness. God will magnify his name as a holy name, for he will sanctify it: <hi type="italic">I will sanctify my name which you have profaned.</hi> When God performs that which he has sworn by his holiness, then he sanctifies his name. The effect of this shall be very happy: <hi type="italic">The heathen shall know that I am the Lord when I shall be sanctified in you before their eyes</hi> and yours. When God proves his own holy name, and his saints praise it, then he is sanctified in them, and this contributes to the propagating of the knowledge of him. Observe, 1. God's reasons of mercy are all fetched from within himself; he will bring his people out of Babylon, not for their sakes, but <hi type="italic">for his own name's sake,</hi> because he will be glorified. 2. God's goodness takes occasion from man's badness to appear so much the more illustrious; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he will sanctify his name by the pardon of sin, because it has been profaned by the commission of sin.
entries.cc9d2df0293c452ed4d76a5109254b0d1efabc46: <div eID="gen19121" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Promise of a New Heart; The Promise of Sanctifying Grace; Promised Blessings Must Be Prayed for. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  587.)</title> <div sID="gen19122" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you. <hi type="super">26</hi> A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. <hi type="super">27</hi> And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">28</hi> And ye shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers; and ye shall be my people, and I will be your God. <hi type="super">29</hi> I will also save you from all your uncleannesses: and I will call for the corn, and will increase it, and lay no famine upon you. <hi type="super">30</hi> And I will multiply the fruit of the tree, and the increase of the field, that ye shall receive no more reproach of famine among the heathen. <hi type="super">31</hi> Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that <hi type="italic">were</hi> not good, and shall loathe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations. <hi type="super">32</hi> Not for your sakes do I <hi type="italic">this,</hi> saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , be it known unto you: be ashamed and confounded for your own ways, O house of Israel. <hi type="super">33</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; In the day that I shall have cleansed you from all your iniquities I will also cause <hi type="italic">you</hi> to dwell in the cities, and the wastes shall be builded. <hi type="super">34</hi> And the desolate land shall be tilled, whereas it lay desolate in the sight of all that passed by. <hi type="super">35</hi> And they shall say, This land that was desolate is become like the garden of Eden; and the waste and desolate and ruined cities <hi type="italic">are become</hi> fenced, <hi type="italic">and</hi> are inhabited. <hi type="super">36</hi> Then the heathen that are left round about you shall know that I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> build the ruined <hi type="italic">places, and</hi> plant that that was desolate: I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and I will do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">37</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I will yet <hi type="italic">for</hi> this be enquired of by the house of Israel, to do <hi type="italic">it</hi> for them; I will increase them with men like a flock. <hi type="super">38</hi> As the holy flock, as the flock of Jerusalem in her solemn feasts; so shall the waste cities be filled with flocks of men: and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen19122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19123" type="x-p"/> The people of God might be discouraged in their hopes of a restoration by the sense not only of their unworthiness of such a favour (which was answered, in the <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.1-Ezek.36.24">foregoing verses</reference>, with this, that God, in doing it, would have an eye to his own glory, not to their worthiness), but of their unfitness for such a favour, being still corrupt and sinful; and that is answered in these verses, with a promise that God would by his grace prepare and qualify them for the mercy and then bestow it on them. And this was in part fulfilled in that wonderful effect which the captivity in Babylon had upon the Jews there, that it effectually cured them of their inclination to idolatry. But it is further intended as a draught of the covenant of grace, and a specimen of those spiritual blessings with which we are blessed in heavenly things by that covenant. As (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.1-Ezek.34.31">ch. xxxiv.</reference>) after a promise of their return the prophecy insensibly slid into a promise of the coming of Christ, the great Shepherd, so here it insensibly slides into a promise of the Spirit, and his gracious influences and operations, which we have as much need of for our sanctification as we have of Christ's merit for our justification. <div eID="gen19123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19124" type="x-p"/> I. God here promises that he will work a good work in them, to qualify them for the good work he intended to bring about for them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25-Ezek.36.27">v. 25-27</reference>. We had promises to the same purport, <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.18-Ezek.11.20">ch. xi. 18-20</reference>. 1. That God would cleanse them from the pollutions of sin (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will sprinkle clean water upon you,</hi> which signifies both the book of Christ sprinkled upon the conscience to purify that and to take away the sense of guilt (as those that were sprinkled with the water of purification were thereby discharged from their ceremonial uncleanness) and the grace of the Spirit sprinkled on the whole soul to purify it from all corrupt inclinations and dispositions, as Naaman was cleansed from his leprosy by dipping in Jordan. Christ was himself clean, else his blood could not have been cleansing to us; and it is a Holy Spirit that makes us holy: <hi type="italic">From all your filthiness and from all your idols will I cleanse you.</hi> And (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.29">v. 29</reference>) <hi type="italic">I will save you from all your uncleannesses.</hi> Sin is defiling, idolatry particularly is so; it renders sinners odious to God and burdensome to themselves. When guilt is pardoned, and the corrupt nature sanctified, then we are cleansed from our filthiness, and there is no other way of being saved from it. This God promises his people here, in order to his being sanctified in them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.23">v. 23</reference>. We cannot sanctify God's name unless he sanctify our hearts, nor live to his glory, but by his grace. 2. That God would give them a <hi type="italic">new heart,</hi> a disposition of mind excellent in itself and vastly different from what it was before. God will work an inward change in order to a universal change. Note, All that have an interest in the new covenant, and a title to the new Jerusalem, have a new heart and a new spirit, and these are necessary in order to their walking in <hi type="italic">newness of life.</hi> This is that <hi type="italic">divine nature</hi> which believers are by the promises made partakers of. 3. That, instead of a <hi type="italic">heart of stone,</hi> insensible and inflexible, unapt to receive any divine impressions and to return any devout affections, God would give a <hi type="italic">heart of flesh,</hi> a soft and tender heart, that has spiritual senses exercised, conscious to itself of spiritual pains and pleasures, and complying in every thing with the will of God. Note, Renewing grace works as great a change in the soul as the turning of a dead stone into living flesh. 4. That since, besides our inclination to sin, we complain of an inability to do our duty, God will <hi type="italic">cause them to walk in his statutes,</hi> will not only show them the way of his statutes before them, but incline them to walk in it, and thoroughly furnish them with wisdom and will, and active powers, for every good work. In order to this he will <hi type="italic">put his Spirit within them,</hi> as a teacher, guide, and sanctifier. Note, God does not force men to walk in his statutes by external violence, but causes them to walk in his statutes by an internal principle. And observe what use we ought to make of this gracious power and principle promised us, and put within us: <hi type="italic">You shall keep my judgments.</hi> If God will do his part according to the promise, we must do ours according to the precept. Note, The promise of God's grace to enable us for our duty should engage and quicken our constant care and endeavour to do our duty. God's promises must drive us to his precepts as our rule, and then his precepts must send us back to his promises for strength, for without his grace we can do nothing. <div eID="gen19124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19125" type="x-p"/> II. God here promises that he will take them into covenant with himself. The sum of the covenant of grace we have, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.28">v. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">You shall be my people, and I will be your God.</hi> It is not, "If you will be my people, I will be your God" (though it is very true that we cannot expect to have God to be to us a God unless we be to him a people), but he has chosen us, and loved us, first, not we him; therefore the condition is of grace, is by promise, as well as the reward; not of merit, not of works: "<hi type="italic">You shall be my people;</hi> I will make you so; I will give you the nature and spirit of my people, and then <hi type="italic">I will be your God.</hi>" And this is the foundation and top-stone of a believer's happiness; it is heaven itself, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Rev. xxi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.7">7</reference>. <div eID="gen19125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19126" type="x-p"/> III. He promises that he will bring about all that good for them which the exigence of their case calls for. When they are thus prepared for mercy, 1. Then they shall return to their possessions and be settled again in them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers.</hi> God will, in bringing them back to it, have an eye not to any merit of theirs, but to the promise made to the fathers; for therefore he gave it to them at first, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.7-Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he is gracious, because he has said that he will be so. This shall follow upon the blessed reformation God would work among them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.33">v. 33</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In the day that I shall have cleansed you from all your iniquities,</hi> and so shall have made you meet for the inheritance, <hi type="italic">I will cause you to dwell in the cities,</hi> and so put you in possession of the inheritance." This is God's method of mercy indeed, first to part men from their sins, and then to restore them to their comforts. 2. Then they shall enjoy a plenty of all good things. When they are saved <hi type="italic">from their uncleanness,</hi> from their sins which kept good things from them, then <hi type="italic">I will call for the corn and will increase it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.29">v. 29</reference>. Plenty comes at God's call, and the plenty he calls for shall be still growing; and when he speaks the word the fruit both of the tree and of the field shall multiply. As the inhabitants multiply the productions shall multiply for their maintenance; for he that sends mouths will send meat. Famine was one of the judgments which they had laboured under, and it had been as much as any a reproach to them, that they should be starved in a land so famed for fruitfulness. But now <hi type="italic">I will lay no famine upon you;</hi> and none are under that rod without having it laid on by him. Then they <hi type="italic">shall receive no more reproach of famine,</hi> shall never be again upbraided with that, nor shall it ever be said that God is a Master that keeps his servants to short allowance. Nay, they shall not only be cleared from the reproach of famine, but they shall have the credit of abundance. The land that had long <hi type="italic">lain desolate in the sight of all that passed by,</hi> that looked upon it, some with contempt and some with compassion, shall again <hi type="italic">be tilled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.34">v. 34</reference>), and, having long lain fallow, it will now be the more fruitful. Observe, God will <hi type="italic">call for the corn</hi> and yet they must <hi type="italic">till the ground</hi> for it. Note, Even promised mercies must be laboured for; for the promise is not to supersede, but to quicken and encourage our industry and endeavour. And such a blessing will God command on the <hi type="italic">hand of the diligent</hi> that all who pass by shall take notice of it, with wonder, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.35">v. 35</reference>. They shall say, "See what a blessed change here is, how <hi type="italic">this land that was desolate</hi> has <hi type="italic">become like the garden of Eden,</hi> the desert turned again into a paradise," Note, God has honours in reserve for his people to be crowned with sufficient to counterbalance the contempt they are now loaded with, and in them he will be honoured. This wonderful increase both of the people of the land and of its products is compared (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.38">v. 38</reference>) to the large flocks of cattle that are brought to Jerusalem, to be sacrificed at one of the solemn feasts. Even the cities that now lie waste shall be filled with <hi type="italic">flocks of men,</hi> not like the flocks with which the pastures are <hi type="italic">covered over</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.13">Ps. lxvi. 13</reference>), but like the holy flock which is brought to the courts of the Lord's house. Note, <hi type="italic">Then</hi> the increase of the numbers of a people is honourable and comfortable indeed when they are all dedicated to God as a holy flock, to be presented to him for <hi type="italic">living sacrifices.</hi> Crowds are a lovely sight in God's temple. <div eID="gen19126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19127" type="x-p"/> IV. He shows what shall be <hi type="italic">the happy effects of this blessed change.</hi> 1. It shall have a happy effect upon the people of God themselves, for it shall bring them to an ingenuous repentance for their sins (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then shall you remember your own evil ways and shall loathe yourselves.</hi> See here what sin is; it is an <hi type="italic">abomination,</hi> a loathsome thing, that abominable thing which the Lord hates. See what is the first step towards repentance; it is <hi type="italic">remembering our own evil ways,</hi> reflecting seriously upon the sins we have committed and being particular in recapitulating them. We must remember against ourselves not only our gross enormities, <hi type="italic">our own evil ways,</hi> but our defects and infirmities, <hi type="italic">our doings that were not good,</hi> not so good as they should have been; not only our direct violations of the law, but our coming short of it. See what is evermore a companion of true repentance, and that is self-loathing, a holy shame and confusion of face: "You shall <hi type="italic">loathe yourselves in your own sight,</hi> seeing how loathsome you have made yourselves in the sight of God." Self-love is at the bottom of sin, which we cannot but blush to see the absurdity of; but our quarrelling with ourselves is in order to our being, upon good grounds, reconciled to ourselves. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> see what is the most powerful inducement to an evangelical repentance, and that is a sense of the mercy of God; when God settles them in the midst of plenty, <hi type="italic">then they shall loathe themselves for their iniquities.</hi> Note, The goodness of God should overcome our badness and <hi type="italic">lead us to repentance.</hi> The more we see of God's readiness to receive us into favour upon our repentance the more reason we shall see to be ashamed of ourselves that we could ever sin against so much love. That heart is hard indeed that will not be thus melted. 2. It shall have a happy effect upon their neighbours, for it shall bring them to a more clear knowledge of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.36">v. 36</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Then the heathen that are left round about you,</hi> that spoke ignorantly of God (for so all those do that speak <hi type="italic">ill</hi> of him) when they saw the land of Israel desolate, shall begin to know better, and to speak more intelligently of God, being convinced that he is able to rebuild the most desolate cities and to replant the most desolate countries, and that, though the course of his favours to his people may be obstructed for a time, they shall not be cut off for ever." They shall be made to know the truth of divine revelation by the exact agreement which they shall discern between God's word which he has spoken to Israel and his works which he has done for them: <hi type="italic">I the Lord have spoken it, and I will do it.</hi> With us saying and doing are two things, but they are not so with God. <div eID="gen19127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19128" type="x-p"/> V. He proposes these things to them, not as the <hi type="italic">recompence</hi> of their merits, but as the return of their prayers. <div eID="gen19128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19129" type="x-p"/> 1. Let them not think that they have deserved it: <hi type="italic">Not for your sakes do I this, be it known to you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.22">v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.32">32</reference>); no, <hi type="italic">be you ashamed and confounded for your own ways.</hi> God is <hi type="italic">doing</hi> this, all this which he has promised; it is as sure to be done as if it were done already, and present events have a tendency towards it. But then, (1.) They must renounce the merit of their own good works, and be brought to acknowledge that it is not for their sakes that it is done; so, when God brought Israel into Canaan the first time, an express <hi type="italic">caveat</hi> was entered against this thought. <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4-Deut.9.6">Deut. ix. 4-6</reference>, <hi type="italic">It is not for thy righteousness.</hi> It is not for the sake of any of their good qualities or good deeds, not because God had any need of them, or expected any benefit by them. No, in showing mercy he acts by prerogative, not for our deserts, but for his own honour. See how emphatically this is expressed: <hi type="italic">Be it known to you,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">not for your sakes,</hi> which intimates that we are apt to entertain a high conceit of our own merits and are with difficulty persuaded to disclaim a confidence in them. But, one way or other, God will make all his favourites to know and own that it is his grace, and not their goodness, his mercy, and not their merit, that made them so; and that therefore not unto them, not unto them, but unto him, is all the glory due. (2.) They must repent of the sin of their own evil ways. They must own that the mercies they receive from God are not only not merited, but that they are a thousand times forfeited; and therefore they must be so far from boasting of their good works that they must be ashamed and confounded for their evil ways, and then they are best prepared for mercy. <div eID="gen19129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19130" type="x-p"/> 2. Yet let them know that they must desire and expect it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will yet for this be enquired of by the house of Israel.</hi> God has spoken, and he will do it, and he will be sought unto for it. He requires that his people should <hi type="italic">seek unto him,</hi> and he will incline their hearts to do it, when he is coming towards them in ways of mercy. (1.) They must pray for it, for by prayer God is sought unto, and enquired after. What is the matter of God's promises must be the matter of our prayers. By asking for the mercy promised we must give glory to the donor, express a value for the gift, own our dependence, and put honour upon prayer which God has put honour upon. Christ himself must ask, and then God will <hi type="italic">give him the heathen for his inheritance,</hi> must <hi type="italic">pray the Father,</hi> and then he will <hi type="italic">send the Comforter;</hi> much more must we ask that we may receive. (2.) They must consult the oracles of God, and thus also God is sought unto and enquired after. The mercy must be, not an act of providence only, but a child of promise; and therefore the promise must be looked at, and prayer made for it with an eye of faith fastened upon the promise, which must be both the guide and the ground of our expectations. Both these ways we find God enquired of by Daniel, in the name of the house of Israel, when he was about to do those great things for them; he consulted the oracles of God, for he <hi type="italic">understood by books,</hi> the book of the prophet Jeremiah, both what was to be expected and when; and then he <hi type="italic">set his face</hi> to seek God by prayer, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2-Dan.9.3">Dan. ix. 2, 3</reference>. Note, Our communion with God must be kept up by the word and prayer in all the operations of his providence concerning us and in both he must be enquired of.  <chapter eID="Ezek.36"/> <div eID="gen19130" type="x-p"/>

entries.4ca12ae01f49b7ca65456a018133fe56204cff72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11713"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 36</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.36.1-Ezek.36.38">Eze 36:1-38</reference>. Israel Avenged of Her Foes, and Restored, First to Inward Holiness, Then to Outward Prosperity.</title> <div sID="gen21215" type="x-p"/> The distinction between Israel and the heathen (as Edom) is: Israel has a covenant relation to God ensuring restoration after chastisement, so that the heathen's hope of getting possession of the elect people's inheritance must fail, and they themselves be made desolate (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.1-Ezek.36.15">Eze 36:1-15</reference>). The reason for the chastisement of Israel was Israel's sin and profanation of God's name (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.16-Ezek.36.21">Eze 36:16-21</reference>). God has good in store for Israel, for His own name's sake, to revive His people; first, by a spiritual renewal of their hearts, and, next, by an external restoration to prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.22-Ezek.36.33">Eze 36:22-33</reference>). The result is that the heathen shall be impressed with the power and goodness of God manifested so palpably towards the restored people (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.34-Ezek.36.38">Eze 36:34-38</reference>).<div eID="gen21215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11713"/><hi type="bold">1-2. mountains of Israel--</hi>in contrast to "Mount Seir" of the previous prophecy. They are here personified; Israel's elevation is moral, not merely physical, as Edom's. Her hills are "the everlasting hills" of Jacob's prophecy (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.26">Ge 49:26</reference>). "The enemy" (Edom, the singled-out representative of all God's foes), with a shout of exultation, "Aha!" had claimed, as the nearest kinsman of Israel (the brother of their father Esau), his vacated inheritance; as much as to say, the so-called "everlasting" inheritance of Israel and of the "hills," which typified the unmoved perpetuity of it (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.1">Psa 125:1</reference>, 2), has come to an end, in spite of the promise of God, and has become "ours" (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13">De 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.15">33:15</reference>). <div eID="gen21216" type="x-p"/>
entries.218ce89265530c285a7bd6bd1c503a6a75ef5929: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11714"/><div sID="gen21217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11714"/>3. Literally, "Because, even because."<div eID="gen21217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swallowed you up--</hi>literally, "panted after" you, as a beast after its prey; implying the greedy cupidity of Edom as to Israel's inheritance (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.1">Psa 56:1</reference>, 2).<div eID="gen21218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lips of talkers--</hi>literally, "lips of the tongue," that is, of the slanderer, the man of tongue. Edom slandered Israel because of the connection of the latter with Jehovah, as though He were unable to save them. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.37">De 28:37</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.24.9">Jr 24:9</reference> had foretold Israel's reproach among the heathen (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.16">Da 9:16</reference>). <div eID="gen21219" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0c3f63338deb6bb136ddb5876f8f4e8eebc5983: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11715"/><div sID="gen21220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11715"/>4. Inanimate creatures are addressed, to imply that the creature also, as it were, groans for deliverance from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.19-Rom.8.21">Ro 8:19-21</reference>) [Polanus]. The completeness of the renewed blessedness of all parts of the land is implied.<div eID="gen21220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">derision--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.79.4">Psa 79:4</reference>). <div eID="gen21221" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d1b988381e40cedd069740184892233bacbd494: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11716"/><div sID="gen21222" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11716"/><hi type="bold">5. to cast it out for a prey--</hi>that is, to take the land for a prey, its inhabitants being cast out. Or the land is compared to a prey cast forth to wild beasts. Fairbairn needlessly alters the Hebrew pointing and translates, "that they may plunder its pasturage." <div eID="gen21222" type="x-p"/>
entries.c40a9d6aabd9d8610e3327633e8dccd1e7bd47db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11717"/><div sID="gen21223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11717"/><hi type="bold">6. the shame of the heathen--</hi>namely, the shame with which the heathen cover you (<reference osisRef="Ps.123.3">Psa 123:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen21223" type="x-p"/>
entries.0576ea9e1d213f138aa38791205b617259d812af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11718"/><div sID="gen21224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11718"/><hi type="bold">7. lifted ... mine hand--</hi>in token of an oath (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.5">Eze 20:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.14.22">Ge 14:22</reference>).<div eID="gen21224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall bear their shame--</hi>a perpetual shame; whereas the "shame" which Israel bore from these heathen was only for a time. <div eID="gen21225" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c99d1f57bce7eba33538ead953555bc2e566c8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11719"/><div sID="gen21226" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11719"/><hi type="bold">8. they are at hand to come--</hi>that is, the Israelites are soon about to return to their land. This proves that the primary reference of the prophecy is to the return from Babylon, which was "at hand," or comparatively near. But this only in part fulfilled the prediction, the full and final blessing in future, and the restoration from Babylon was an earnest of it. <div eID="gen21226" type="x-p"/>
entries.6325bad497775519439e2a0ad53ea191461d22f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11720"/><div sID="gen21227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11720"/><hi type="bold">10. wastes builded--</hi><reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Is 58:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.4">61:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>, 12, 14, where, as here (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>), the names of David, Messiah's type, and Edom, Israel's foe, are introduced in connection with the coming restoration. <div eID="gen21227" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b240d8a1f0a2c9ee91f1d03ec33b7c1c3df5fd4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11721"/><div sID="gen21228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11721"/><hi type="bold">11. do better ... than at your beginnings--</hi>as in the case of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.42.12">Job 42:12</reference>). Whereas the heathen nations fall irrevocably, Israel shall be more than restored; its last estate shall exceed even its first. <div eID="gen21228" type="x-p"/>
entries.599c16b5462236587250145bd1e80083700206f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11722"/><div sID="gen21229" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11722"/><hi type="bold">12. to walk upon you--</hi>O mountains of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.8">Eze 36:8</reference>)!<div eID="gen21229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thee ... thou--</hi>change from plural to singular: O hill of Zion, singled out from the other mountains of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.26">Eze 34:26</reference>); or land.<div eID="gen21230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shall no more ... bereave them of men--</hi>Thou shalt no more provoke God to bereave them of children (so the ellipsis ought to be supplied, as Ezekiel probably alludes to <reference osisRef="Jer.15.7">Jr 15:7</reference>, "I will bereave them of children"). <div eID="gen21231" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c1e8c18676adb0ad58842ba24d450297e6febfb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11723"/><div sID="gen21232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11723"/><hi type="bold">13. Thou land devourest up men--</hi>alluding to the words of the spies (<reference osisRef="Num.13.32">Nu 13:32</reference>). The land personified is represented as doing that which was done in it. Like an unnatural mother it devoured, that is, it was the grave of its people; of the Canaanites, its former possessors, through mutual wars, and finally by the sword of Israel; and now, of the Jews, through internal and external ills; for example, wars, famine (to which <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.30">Eze 36:30</reference>, "reproach of famine among the heathen," implies the allusion here is). <div eID="gen21232" type="x-p"/>
entries.e05f55247bea580b9ec3c89139bcbe3377119a49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11724"/><div sID="gen21233" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11724"/><hi type="bold">14. bereave--</hi>so the Keri, or Hebrew Margin reads, to correspond to "bereave" in <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.13">Eze 36:13</reference>; but "cause to fall" or "stumble," in the Hebrew text or Chetib, being the more difficult reading, is the one least likely to come from a corrector; also, it forms a good transition to the next subject, namely, the moral cause of the people's calamities, namely, their falls, or stumblings through sin. The latter ceasing, the former also cease. So the same expression follows in <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.15">Eze 36:15</reference>, "Neither shalt thou cause thy nations to fall any more." <div eID="gen21233" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4eee440606fe20fff0466445fd76692f727373a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11725"/><div sID="gen21234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11725"/><hi type="bold">17. removed woman--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.15.19">Le 15:19</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen21234" type="x-p"/>
entries.59a3957a807c69503021d1a06281471157166888: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11726"/><div sID="gen21235" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11726"/>18-19. The reason for their removal was their sin, which God's holiness could not let pass unpunished; just as a woman's legal uncleanness was the reason for her being separated from the congregation. <div eID="gen21235" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f297c45094b8fdfa7dba8a19fc7d94d1c9a9905: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11727"/><div sID="gen21236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11727"/><hi type="bold">20. profaned my holy name, when they--</hi>the heathen<div eID="gen21236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">said to them--</hi>the Israelites.<div eID="gen21237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">These, &c.--</hi>The Israelites gave a handle of reproach to the heathen against God, who would naturally say, These who take usury, oppress, commit adultery, &c., and who, in such an abject plight, are "gone forth" as exiles "out of His land," are specimens of what Jehovah can or will effect, for His people, and show what kind of a God this so-called holy, omnipotent, covenant-keeping God must be! (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Is 52:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.24">Ro 2:24</reference>). <div eID="gen21238" type="x-p"/>
entries.19a58cf2e1d07257a363c585296f49bd90199e6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11728"/><div sID="gen21239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11728"/><hi type="bold">21. I had pity for mine holy name--</hi>that is, I felt pity for it; God's own name, so dishonored, was the primary object of His pitying concern; then His people, secondarily, through His concern for it [Fairbairn]. <div eID="gen21239" type="x-p"/>
entries.f59e5abc297bd2fc8180a2b1202b1d8a1f97efe4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11729"/><div sID="gen21240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11729"/><hi type="bold">22. not ... for your sakes--</hi>that is, not for any merit in you; for, on the contrary, on your part, there is everything to call down continued severity (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.9.5">De 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.6">6</reference>). The sole and sure ground of hope was God's regard to "His own name," as the God of covenant grace (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>), which He must vindicate from the dishonor brought on it by the Jews, before the heathen. <div eID="gen21240" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe5c626fff6e8db391831a03dd55fb17b3b9e29a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11730"/><div sID="gen21241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11730"/><hi type="bold">23. sanctify--</hi>vindicate and manifest as holy, in opposition to the heathen reproaches of it brought on by the Jews' sins and their punishment (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.20">Eze 36:20</reference>).<div eID="gen21241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctified in you--</hi>that is, in respect of you; I shall be regarded in their eyes as the Holy One, and righteous in My dealings towards you (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.41">Eze 20:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.22">28:22</reference>). <div eID="gen21242" type="x-p"/>
entries.316412fdfab45a1105651e3cc83fdebcec64b92c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11731"/><div sID="gen21243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11731"/>24. Fulfilled primarily in the restoration from Babylon; ultimately to be so in the restoration "from all countries." <div eID="gen21243" type="x-p"/>
entries.34f7a953c66630a37079ec158ac8cc93e9e8fca3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11732"/><div sID="gen21244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11732"/>25. The external restoration must be preceded by an internal one. The change in their condition must not be superficial, but must be based on a radical renewal of the heart. Then the heathen, understanding from the regenerated lives of God's people how holy God is, would perceive Israel's past troubles to have been only the necessary vindications of His righteousness. Thus God's name would be "sanctified" before the heathen, and God's people be prepared for outward blessings.<div eID="gen21244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sprinkle ... water--</hi>phraseology taken from the law; namely, the water mixed with the ashes of a heifer sprinkled with a hyssop on the unclean (<reference osisRef="Num.19.9-Num.19.18">Nu 19:9-18</reference>); the thing signified being the cleansing blood of Christ sprinkled on the conscience and heart (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">He 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">10:22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.33.8">Jr 33:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.26">Ep 5:26</reference>).<div eID="gen21245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from all your idols--</hi>Literal idolatry has ceased among the Jews ever since the captivity; so far, the prophecy has been already fulfilled; but "cleansing from all their idols," for example, covetousness, prejudices against Jesus of Nazareth, is yet future. <div eID="gen21246" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a8b4d189b419fbfa68a094e056377829ec38928: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11733"/><div sID="gen21247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11733"/><hi type="bold">26. new heart--</hi>mind and will.<div eID="gen21247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit--</hi>motive and principle of action.<div eID="gen21248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stony heart--</hi>unimpressible in serious things; like the "stony ground" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.5">Mt 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.20">20</reference>), unfit for receiving the good seed so as to bring forth fruit.<div eID="gen21249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heart of flesh--</hi>not "carnal" in opposition to "spiritual"; but impressible and docile, fit for receiving the good seed. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.31">Eze 18:31</reference> they are commanded, "Make you a new heart, and a new spirit." Here God says, "A new heart will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you." Thus the responsibility of man, and the sovereign grace of God, are shown to be coexistent. Man cannot make himself a new heart unless God gives it (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.12">Php 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen21250" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f222d57cb92327655eaf6573ee94809765b1650: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11734"/><div sID="gen21251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11734"/><hi type="bold">27. my spirit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.19">Eze 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.39">Jr 32:39</reference>). The partial reformation at the return from Babylon (<reference osisRef="Ezra.10.6">Ezr 10:6</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Neh.8.1-Neh.9.38">Ne 8:1-9:38</reference>) was an earnest of the full renewal hereafter under Messiah. <div eID="gen21251" type="x-p"/>
entries.46e6027ce72e40ee7751f0212dc1cf1463f72891: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11735"/><div sID="gen21252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11735"/><hi type="bold">28. ye ... my people, ... I ... your God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.20">Eze 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.22">Jr 30:22</reference>). <div eID="gen21252" type="x-p"/>
entries.a78e12392b347f0e988d685e55386140e28f2b6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11736"/><div sID="gen21253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11736"/><hi type="bold">29. save ... from all ... uncleannesses--</hi>the province of Jesus, according to the signification of His name (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Mt 1:21</reference>). To be specially exercised in behalf of the Jews in the latter days (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>).<div eID="gen21253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call for ... corn--</hi>as a master "calls for" a servant; all the powers and productions of nature are the servants of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.16">Psa 105:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.8.8">Mt 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.9">9</reference>). Compare as to the subordination of all the intermediate agents to the Great First Cause, who will give "corn" and all good things to His people, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.21">Ho 2:21</reference>, 22; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.12">Zec 8:12</reference>. <div eID="gen21254" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8883e0c290c9c1b997bf1fd86eed51faeef6397: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11737"/><div sID="gen21255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11737"/><hi type="bold">30. no more reproach of famine among the heathen--</hi>to which their taunt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.13">Eze 36:13</reference>), "Thou land devourest up men," in part referred. <div eID="gen21255" type="x-p"/>
entries.b30fdb1e8f9bf11f143140be34bf50da6d605cb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11738"/><div sID="gen21256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11738"/><hi type="bold">31. remember your ... evil ways--</hi>with shame and loathing. The unexpected grace and love of God, manifested in Christ to Israel, shall melt the people into true repentance, which mere legal fear could not (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.61">Eze 16:61</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">63</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.33.8">Jr 33:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen21256" type="x-p"/>
entries.e70a4e1b6fd840b0509efdcafb053c48ac61c4df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11739"/><div sID="gen21257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11739"/><hi type="bold">35. they shall say--</hi>The heathen, who once made Israel's desolation a ground of reproach against the name of Jehovah Himself (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.20">Eze 36:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.21">21</reference>); but now He so vindicates its sanctity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.22">Eze 36:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.23">23</reference>) that these same heathen are constrained to acknowledge Israel's more than renewed blessedness to be God's own work, and a ground for glorifying His name (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.36">Eze 36:36</reference>).<div eID="gen21257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Eden--</hi>as Tyre (the type of the world powers in general: so Assyria, a cedar "in the garden of God, Eden," <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.8">Eze 31:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.9">9</reference>), in original advantages, had been compared to "Eden, the garden of God" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.13">Eze 28:13</reference>), from which she had fallen irrecoverably; so Israel, once desolate, is to be as "the garden of Eden" (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.3">Is 51:3</reference>), and is to be so unchangeably. <div eID="gen21258" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d1b17fbd9f607cf8bbc7f47a29166a20892e787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11740"/><div sID="gen21259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11740"/><hi type="bold">36. Lord ... spoken ... do it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.23.19">Nu 23:19</reference>). <div eID="gen21259" type="x-p"/>
entries.a52f9c20071874cb150ef689a92a8749e68a94c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11741"/><div sID="gen21260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11741"/><hi type="bold">37. I will yet for this be inquired of--</hi>so as to grant it. On former occasions He had refused to be inquired of by Israel because the inquirers were not in a fit condition of mind to receive a blessing (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Eze 14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.3">20:3</reference>). But hereafter, as in the restoration from Babylon (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.1-Neh.9.38">Ne 8:1-9:38</reference>; Da 9:3-20, 21, 23), God will prepare His people's hearts (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.26">Eze 36:26</reference>) to pray aright for the blessings which He is about to give (Psa 102:13-17, 20; Zec 12:10-14; 13:<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1</reference>).<div eID="gen21260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like a flock--</hi>resuming the image (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.31">31</reference>). <div eID="gen21261" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc12eaa8912158fa2e5c399e774596d1c00c7c7c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11742"/><div sID="gen21262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11742"/><hi type="bold">38. As the holy flock--</hi>the great flock of choice animals for sacrifice, brought up to Jerusalem at the three great yearly festivals, the passover, pentecost, and feast of the tabernacles. <chapter eID="Ezek.36"/>

entries.e5fcce243cb8d5db502e5e394aedfd0000575c2b: <div eID="gen32338" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32339" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32340" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32340" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32339" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32341" type="x-p"/> The Edomites or Idumeans, during the Babylonish captivity, took possession of the mountainous parts of Judea, and the fortresses which commanded the country, intending to exclude the Jews if ever they should return from their captivity. The prophet therefore, by a beautiful personification, addresses the mountains of Israel; and, ascribing to them passions and emotions similar to those of his own breast, consoles them with the prospect of being soon rid of those usurping foes; of being freed from the dishonor of idols under which they groaned; and of flourishing again in their ancient glory under their rightful owners, <reference osisRef="Eze.36.1-Eze.36.15">Eze 36:1-15</reference>. The idolatry and other sins of the Jews are then declared to be the cause of their captivity and dispersion, <reference osisRef="Eze.36.16-Eze.36.20">Eze 36:16-20</reference>; from which however they are promised a deliverance in terms of great force and beauty, vv. 21-38. This chapter contains also, under the type of the happy condition of the Israelites after their restoration from the Babylonish captivity, a glorious prophecy of the rich blessings of the Gospel dispensation. <div eID="gen32341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32342" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32343" type="x-p"/> Prophesy unto the mountains of Israel - This is a part of the preceding prophecy though it chiefly concerns the Jews. In it they are encouraged to expect a glorious restoration, and that none of the evil wishes of their adversaries should take place against them.
entries.302870e8e258b0ca2a76af59b1125107c1b943c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32344" type="x-p"/> Because the enemy hath said - The Idumeans thought they would shortly be put in possession of all the strong places of Israel; the ancient high places shall be ours.
